sample.extracted_statement: The most wise Creator creates and governs all things with perfect order, harmoniously fashioning his works and revealing his laws, doctrines, and promises.
sample.source_text:
Things* and to the Mind of the speaker, and to the minds of the hearers or readers. Now since concepts and words are to be conformed to things, the true rationale of Method consists in this conformity. And he who does not know the order and harmony of things, has no claim to the praise of science, nor even to its name. Such a man is the Physicist, the Astronomer, the Geographer, the Arithmetician, the Musician, etc., who is ignorant of the order of things — it is needless to elaborate further. There is no Kingdom, no City, no Church, no School, no household *without Order*. What kind of assembly will there be, what kind of Oration, or what other divine worship, without *order*? And who will deem a man in his right mind who utters only incoherent words with no order at all?
The necessity of Method, therefore, these arguments plainly show:
1. The most wise Creator and Governor of the world creates and governs all things with perfect order: Harmoniously God has fashioned all his works: Harmoniously he has revealed his Laws, doctrines, and promises; and the Truth of concepts and Words consists in their conformity to the things themselves (as was said before): the harmony of things True, Good, and To-be-done is given: Harmoniously, therefore, things are to be understood, loved, and done. Will he not sin who worships God in the place and order of a creature, and the creature in the place of God? Who assigns to earthly things the primacy, and to heavenly things the secondary place; who puts the end in the place of the means, and the means in the place of the end? Who prefers the body to the soul, and carnal things to spiritual?
2. *He who knows things methodically and in their proper order* knows them not only as true, but as it were pregnant and full of evidence, pointing to further truths; he knows them. For truth is a concatenation; and he who knows few things in their proper order, will all the more easily and truly understand many things. Method is a great aid both to understanding and to memory. Beginning from the radical or fundamental things, the investigation of their consequences and of the smallest things becomes easier. And one may scarcely hope that he will proceed well who begins badly: From one false thing very many things follow. And it is worthy of note that Relations are for the most part founded in order, and in many sciences the parts hold such great relations, that those ignorant of them can explain very few things correctly.
3. But he who knows things rightly by order and method, knows them *clearly*: Truths rightly ordered shed light upon one another: and from the due placing of things and words the understanding receives a fuller satisfaction than from the subtleties of very many syllogisms. And he who does not perceive truths harmoniously and methodically holds them too loosely and slipperily, because he does not sufficiently perceive the amiable concord and mutual light by which they shine upon one another. He who perceives natural truths rightly in their own place has no small advantage thereby, from which he may the more easily and firmly receive supernatural truths.
